q: What does Hermes do at build time that a plain engine does on the phone at every start?
options: It reads your JavaScript and turns it into bytecode
It downloads your JavaScript from a server
why: Hermes compiles your JavaScript into bytecode when you build the app. At start the phone only loads and runs it, so there is less to read.

q: The phone provides the Hermes engine, so your app file does not contain it.
why: No. Hermes is packed inside your app, and a matching Hermes is built for each React Native release. Bytecode fits only the exact engine that reads it.

q: Which of these are good ways to check Hermes and its speed benefit?
options: Check that global.HermesInternal is not empty
Compare release builds on the same phone, before and after
Time the start with the dev server running on a laptop
Make sure the .hbc bundle is the one that loads
why: HermesInternal shows the engine is there, the .hbc bundle shows the code is precompiled, and a release build comparison shows the speed. A dev build says little about the shipped app.

q: A screen is slow because it sorts 50,000 items on every render. What fixes it?
options: Do the sort once or move it elsewhere. Hermes does not fix slow code you wrote
Switch to Hermes V1, which makes all code fast
Use more console.log calls to find the slow line
why: Hermes helps loading and memory. Your own heavy work stays heavy. The release post itself says the gains strongly depend on the details of your app.

q: Put these Hermes versions in the order they came in React Native.
items: 0.82: Hermes V1 can be turned on as an opt in
why: 0.70 made Hermes the default, 0.82 added Hermes V1 as an experimental opt in, and 0.84 made Hermes V1 the default on iOS and Android.

q: Compiled Hermes code is saved in a file that ends in .______ (three letters).
why: Hermes bytecode files end in .hbc. If you load your bundle in an unusual way, confirm that this precompiled file is the one that loads.
